Three things you learned last week

Our mini project: the Homework Helper Input a Python homework. A syntax error is reported as a syntax error; only if the syntax passes does it write feedback containing "Strengths:" and "Improvements:". If the maximum generations (including the first) is reached and the feedback still fails, it reports not passed.
Workflow version (1-A): check_syntax checks syntax (grammar only, does not run it) → give_feedback writes the feedback (the only step that uses AI) → check_format checks the format (if it fails, rewrite a limited number of times; report when the limit is reached).
Agent version (1-B): the AI picks from its toolbox: run_code (runs the homework), check_indent (checks indentation), read_spec (reads the assignment requirements).

Agent = model + tools + loop

The model decides, a tool runs, the result comes back and the model decides again, until the model's reply is complete or a limit is reached.

Flow control and AI judgment

Steps that must run go into the workflow; things that need judgment go to the agent. Put an agent in one station of the workflow to combine fixed steps with model judgment.

Two common ways to get tools

A function you wrote yourself, or one plugged in through an MCP socket.

No quiz. We are just putting last week's material back on the table. Everything new today attaches to these three things.

For anyone who missed last week: the summary box above is what we keep building across both sessions. The workflow version checks syntax first; if it passes, it writes feedback and checks the format, and a syntax error is reported directly. The agent version decides for itself whether to run the homework and read the assignment. Today we give it a handbook, and at the end we decide where each feature belongs.

Last week's leftover problem: feedback style hard-coded

Last week's 1-B helper agent: in this example the model, the toolbox, and the feedback style are all set in one piece of code
from langchain.agents import create_agentagent = create_agent(    model,    tools=[run_code, check_indent, read_spec],    system_prompt="You are a Python homework helper with a gentle tone, "                  "strengths first, then improvements...",)

Toolbox: run_code actually runs the homework, check_indent checks indentation, read_spec reads the assignment requirements; the feedback style is written on this line of system_prompt .

  • The officer says "be stricter at midterm" → edit the code and rerun
  • To support several styles → you must maintain several sets of prompt text
  • Is there a way to keep the code unchanged and just swap one sheet of paper?

This agent's feedback style is written inside the code. When the officer says "be stricter at midterm", you have to edit the code and rerun. To support several styles, you have to maintain several sets of prompt text. Is there a way to keep the code unchanged and just swap one sheet of paper?

What do you give a new colleague on day one?

You don't rewire a new colleague's brain. You hand them a handbook.

Skill A work handbook for the AI: a folder holding one SKILL.md text file that describes how to do a certain kind of task. The AI reads it and tries to follow it. Not one line of code changes.[1]

You don't rewire a new colleague's brain. You hand them a handbook. A Skill is a work handbook for the AI: a folder holding one SKILL.md text file that describes how to do a certain kind of task. The AI reads it and tries to follow it. Not one line of code changes [1].

Request to enterWrite your prediction firstWhat to check after running

Midterm exam, official grading: please review strictlyWhich one will it pick? What is the reason?Compare with the chosen handbook's description
Keep the output of each request once: confirm the requests differ and the cards do not, then compare the picks. The body is only edited on the next slide.

Colab2-A: Part 2, Experiment A: run each of the two requests once; stop before Experiment B when done

About 3 minutes. Don't change the request, the homework, and the handbook all at once. The model may pick a different handbook than you predicted; have students compare against the actual cards and output, and don't rerun until it matches the prediction. A pick that isn't ideal doesn't affect the next experiment, B, because B has the program choose the gentle handbook directly.

In class, keep one pick result for the beginner request and one for the midterm request, and confirm the outputs show different requests and identical cards. Pressing Run all, or rerunning the same default value, only gives the baseline and does not count as the comparison. Picking the same handbook both times is still a valid observation; no need to rerun until the result differs.

About 5 minutes. The beginner request is fixed and the program picks friendly-feedback directly, which removes the picking variable. Run once with the default rules, then add rule 5 under rule 4 (a specified closing sentence; leave the first four unchanged), and compare the loaded rules and the feedback. Keep the output from before and after the rule change. In the second run, first check that "the handbook loaded this time includes the new closing rule" is True. One naming check, three placements

Confirm the shared rule first, then look at the same homework: variables, functions, and parameters must be lowercase with underscores; digits are allowed, and constants are not exempt.

PlacementWho checksWho decides to run it
A: the handbook states the check rulesThe model judges from the textThe program asks the model to check
B: the handbook tells the AI to call a script toolPython scriptagent
C: the workflow always calls the same scriptThe same Python scriptThe outer workflow
For example: my_score and score2 pass; myScore and MAX_SCORE do not. Circle the problems yourself first, then look at the script's answer.
Colab2-B: Part 1: predict first, then run; A, B, and C use the same homework and the same rule

You can open with: "The three versions use the same homework and the same naming rule. What changes is who does the checking and who decides when it runs." Let students circle the problems before they see the script's answer. Constants are not exempt in this exercise; that is not a naming standard for all Python projects.

Colab2-B: Part 5: explain the difference between A, B, and C with the two questions

Wrap up sentence by sentence: "From A to B, the check moves from the model to a script; from B to C, the check method is the same, but the workflow now guarantees it runs." Ask students to point out the script that B and C share, so code, tool, Skill, and workflow are not treated as mutually exclusive categories. Then ask: if the rule today were that every homework must have its naming checked, which one would you choose? This check step needs no model, but that does not mean the whole feedback system never uses a model.

In this real Colab run, all three versions were correct and identical, and A did not fail. The difference is in execution control and model calls. A makes one model response per run, B made two per run this time (the tool request and the final reply), and C makes zero in this step; this is not a guarantee of fixed call counts for every input. B's "keeps every item" compares the set of parsed line numbers and names, not the whole reply word for word.

Predict firstThen observe

Prompt injection: Untrusted text carries instructions that try to pull the model off its original task. If it doesn't happen this time, still check the tool record and the permissions.

This is a paired permission experiment. We do not swap in a safe handbook, so we do not change two variables at once. Shell, encodings, and scanners are optional.

Three habits before using an external Skill

HabitYou can do it today
Check the contentsRead SKILL.md; check whether attached scripts do anything beyond the task
Limit permissionsGive it only the tools the task needs; don't casually hand over abilities such as reading keys or sending email
Confirm the source and versionPrefer trusted sources and record the version you use; read the contents even from official sources

Combining workflow and agent: wiring handbooks and tools

Colab2-D Parts 1-2: integration experiment: first check the homework against its assignment, then look at the chosen handbook, the tools the agent asked for (tools_used), and the format result

The outer layer fixes the required steps; the inner agent picks tools. A failed format can be sent back for a rewrite; if the maximum generations (including the first) is reached and it still fails, it reports not passed.

This diagram shows the main path and leaves out skill_loader and the branches; the connection points are explained on the next slide. 2-D uses its own default handbook. First run Parts 1-2 with a syntactically valid sample, check the assignment that matches this homework, then observe the handbook, the model's tool requests (tools_used), and the format result. 2-D records only tool names and does not print raw tool returns. The assignment requirements enter State with this input, and read_spec reads from the same State; it does not rewrite the shared assignment file that all homework uses. A syntax error is reported directly. Feedback generations include the first one, and when the limit is reached and it still fails, report not passed; do not treat failed feedback as a success.

Colab2-D: Parts 1-2: check this assignment, the handbook, and the tool connection points; the next slide practices saving and resuming

This section is 15 minutes: about 7 for integration and about 8 for the three saved states. Read the results first; leave API details for after class. The outer workflow controls the required steps; the inner agent judges and picks tools.

Order of operations: first confirm this homework and its assignment requirements, then run. The assignment and the code are saved into State together, and read_spec reads the assignment from this State; when you resume from a save, it reuses the same assignment and does not read the global assignment file that other homework uses. Passing the format check only checks text structure; whether the assignment is understood and the feedback is correct still has to be checked. An earlier version once read the shared addition assignment; that output is kept as historical evidence and is not treated as a verified result of the new version.

Feature 1: fetching homework from GitHub

The design goal is to collect homework from GitHub; 2-E first demonstrates the service connection with 5 built-in sample homeworks.

ItemDesign goalWhat 2-E does now
Data sourceThe specified repo and files on GitHub5 students and their homework in a Python dictionary
Tool interfaceConnect the GitHub API, or adapt a compatible MCP toolCustom MCP: list_homework, get_homework
Who runs itA fixed fetch can be called directly by the workflowThe fetch_homework node gets the roster first, then each submission's code
The MCP connection is real; the data source is simulated.
2-E does not yet read students' homework from GitHub; sending email only writes to a simulated outbox.

To connect real GitHub, you need to adapt tool names, parameters, and return formats; a fetch with a known path can be done by plain code.

Start with: "The slides' requirement is to collect homework from GitHub. To learn service connection and workflow division of labor first, the notebook simulates the data source with five built-in sample homeworks." In 2-E, homework_mcp.py stores the students, fake mailboxes, and code in one dictionary; list_homework returns the roster, and get_homework returns the code by name. The fetch_homework node in multi_agent.py calls the two tools in order in plain code, then hands off to the later review. Both stdio and HTTP run on the same Colab machine and do not yet connect to students' repos; swapping the MCP URL for any GitHub server will not be automatically compatible, because the tool interface has to match too. About 3 minutes. This absorbs the handoff reminder from the original division-of-labor principles slide: verification needs the assignment, the homework, and the draft, and cannot look at an isolated result. In the 2-E API output at d2c81b7, Fiona's feedback was judged as passing, but it suggested changing total += s to four spaces while also asking for four spaces per level, without making the nesting relationship between the for line and the statement inside the loop clear. The original two-space/eight-space program still parses; putting both the for line and its inner statement at four spaces would cause an IndentationError. Do not wrongly claim that changing that one line alone is certain to be a syntax error. This example shows that a model auditor can miss an ambiguity in a suggested change; when reviewing, check the full revised program and rerun syntax and behavior tests.

The division of labor in the cloud: where each box lives

Details are in "Supplementary: moving to the cloud" (this appendix) Colab2-E: exercises 1-2 run the division of labor with a simulated repo and a send-email tool; exercise 3 wraps it as an API (the self-built container route)

Code, handbooks, and scripts travel with the container; changing data goes into a database; keys go into a vault; other people's abilities are connected over the network.

A deployment concept diagram for optional reading after class; finish the core exercises first, then read the deployment details as needed.

Move the full division-of-labor diagram to the cloud and each box lives in a different place. In the middle is "your container": the API (others send homework in by URL), the outer workflow (code), the feedback agent, the local tools, plus skills/ and scripts/, which are packaged into the image together with the code; at deploy time, check the versions of the code, handbooks, and attachments. The container can sit on a service like Cloud Run, or be handed to LangSmith Deployment to host. The two routes have different APIs: a self-built container runs server.py and so has POST /batch; the hosted platform reads the graph that langgraph.json points to and uses the platform's built-in threads/runs API.

Data that changes does not live in the container, because cloud instances can restart or be replaced: each thread_id's State, the emails waiting for a person's confirmation, and the vector data RAG searches all go in a database (for example Postgres). The model's API key and OAuth token go in a vault (Secret Manager) and only become environment variables at deploy time.

Other people's abilities come in over the network: the model itself is someone else's API; fetching homework from GitHub and sending email are remote MCP (2-E uses one homework repo server that also sends email); run_code runs code that students wrote, so after launch it must go in a sandbox. Alongside are a task queue (200 submissions waiting) and a Trace/Eval dashboard (every step visible, an automatic test after each change).

Compared with 2-E: the graph always loads friendly-feedback when it is built, and there is no skill_loader node; review_one checks syntax first, and only if it passes does the agent generate feedback, which then goes to feedback verification. This differs from 2-D's handbook picking and format-retry flow. Passing verification means the feedback is acceptable, not that the student's homework is correct; a syntax-error notice can pass too. In this run, Chloe made no tool call but the model was called twice (review and verification), so you cannot say her code was run. Postgres, remote services, and isolated environments in the diagram are deployment targets; Colab still uses SQLite and local simulated services.

In ColabIn the cloud
Modelgoogle.colab.ai: availability depends on the Colab account and quotaThe model credentials used in the deployment environment go in the cloud's password vault (Secret Manager), and the code reads them from environment variables
Files/content/review-bot/: lost when the runtime is deleted or rebuiltCode, skills/, scripts/ are packed together into a container

Colab2-E: the pre-launch check in exercise 4 looks at whether the key comes from an environment variable; seeing ⚠️ when using Colab's built-in model is normal. To practice keeping them separate: add GOOGLE_API_KEY under 🔑 Secrets, set the environment setting to gemini, and rerun

Container: packs the code and the dependencies it needs, so a compatible environment can more easily reproduce the run conditions.

First is the model: google.colab.ai exists only inside Colab, so at deployment you need to set up a model service and credentials. A key must not be written in code or in SKILL.md; it goes in the cloud's Secret Manager and becomes an environment variable at deployment.

Second is files: Colab's /content runtime is wiped when it is deleted or rebuilt. To go to the cloud, package the code, the skills/ folder, and scripts/ together into a container image, and version-control the handbooks along with the code.

Third is memory: the checkpointer shown in 2-D lives on that one Colab machine. Cloud instances can restart or be replaced, so switch to a checkpointer that stores in a database, such as PostgresSaver, so the same thread_id can be picked up again [13]. The trigger changes too: it is no longer you pressing Run, but an HTTP API, a schedule, or a webhook.

A LangGraph project going to the cloud needs a packing slip, langgraph.json: dependencies says what to install, graphs says "which variable in which file is the graph", and env says where the environment variables come from [12].

dependencies set to "." points at the local project's dependencies; after the build, confirm skills/ and scripts/ are complete, and at deploy time check the versions of the code, handbooks, and attachments. langgraph dev opens an API and a Studio view on your machine; get it running there first. langgraph build packages a Docker image from langgraph.json (it does not use the repo's Dockerfile, and there is no POST /batch); before deploying you still need to check the target platform, dependencies, and storage settings. 2-E's Dockerfile takes the self-built container route: after docker build, uvicorn starts server.py, and the saved State is still SQLite inside the container. .env is for local use only; in production put the keys in Secret Manager.

Reviewing 200 at once: Send

from langgraph.types import Send def dispatch(state):    # Each homework gets its own data a = {student, email, code}, run the same node    return [Send("review_one", a) for a in state["roster"]] builder.add_conditional_edges("fetch_homework", dispatch, ["review_one"]) # Run at most 20 at a time; the rest wait in linegraph.invoke(inputs, config={"max_concurrency": 20})

Gather the results in a field typed Annotated[list, operator.add] and you have map-reduce [14].

  • A clean desk for each one: avoids carrying over the previous conversation; you still need to check that student IDs match results
  • Set a parallel cap: a model API has a per-minute limit, and sending too many requests at once can hit the quota
  • Do the math first: measure the calls and tokens per submission first, then estimate the batch total; parallelism does not mean a fixed cost multiple

Colab2-E: exercise 2 first reviews one, then five; 200 is an extended scenario, and parallel performance has to be measured separately

Send: in the flow you say "this node, one run for each item in this list", and LangGraph schedules it under the parallel limit.

Send dispatches independent inputs to the same node; the node can call the same agent, and no new role is required. Set a parallel cap, keep the student ID, and measure the cost per submission and for the whole batch. Actual speed is still limited by the model and resources.

In the saved output, exercise 2 reviewed only Chloe's one submission; the API exercise then reviewed five. We have not saved a parallel-speed comparison under the same conditions, so do not claim from this that parallelism speeds things up or that 200 have been reviewed.

Skill HandbooksCode · Text · ScriptsSecurity & IntegrationSystem DesignSupplementary53 / 57

Wait for confirmation before sending: interrupt()

from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command def confirm_before_send(state):    emails = [...]# each one's student, email, verification result, feedback    decision = interrupt({"emails_to_send": emails,                      "options": ["Send all", "Send only verified", "Send none"]})    return {"decision": decision}   # Send none → end directly; anything else → send node (send_email is an MCP tool) # After the officer reads the content in the back office and chooses:graph.invoke(Command(resume="Send only verified"),             config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "midterm-batch-1"}})
  • interrupt saves State into the checkpointer and then pauses; during the wait you must keep a save that can be resumed [15]
  • In deployment, use a durable checkpointer, and store the data so that progress waiting for confirmation is not lost after a restart

Colab2-E: exercise 2, steps 1-2: stop at confirm_before_send with interrupt(), then continue with Command(resume=...) after choosing; the API in exercise 3 does the same thing with two requests (no real email is sent in class)

When confirming, check the suggested edits; even if verification passed, it may have misjudged the indentation level.

Sending email is irreversible, so Stop 4 said to add a human confirmation on the outside. LangGraph's way is interrupt: execution reaches this point, saves State into the checkpointer, pauses, and returns what a person should look at; after the person confirms, Command(resume=...) with the same thread_id tells it to continue, and the resume value becomes the return value of interrupt [15]. In 2-E the resume value can only be one of three: "Send all", "Send only verified", or "Send none"; choosing "Send none" ends right away without entering the send node.

This is also why the cloud needs a durable checkpointer: an officer may press confirm three days later, and the instance may have been replaced during the wait. The official docs also recommend a durable checkpointer for production [15].

In this run of 2-E, Fiona's feedback had an ambiguity about the indentation level, was still judged as passing by the model, and was recorded as simulated-sent after confirmation. Human confirmation also exists to check that the content is correct, not just to look at the pass flag or press send. Read the whole suggestion; when it touches program structure, check the full revised program, and only then decide to send, send back, or not send.

Visible (check after acting)
  • Trace: every step of every homework leaves a record, so when something fails you can find which step
  • Eval in CI: following the approach in "Optional: checking a pure agent with code", write separate cases for the deployed graph (the syntax-error branch, verification failing, stopping at confirm-before-send), run them automatically on every handbook or code change, and judge whether to accept the change by your team's threshold
  • Cost: how many tokens each homework costs, checked once a day
Containable (permissions and habits)
  • Give each tool only the permissions it needs: the review agent can't get the send-email tool, and send_email is called only by the send node
  • run_code runs in an isolated environment: time-limited, memory-limited, no network
  • Before a third-party Skill enters the repo, review it with 2-C's three habits and pin the version
  • Keys live only in Secret Manager, never in SKILL.md, code, or git
  • In this example, wait for human confirmation with interrupt before sending email

Colab2-E: the pre-launch check in exercise 4 does keys, a simple scan of third-party Skills, and the deployment files in one go

Going to the cloud is not running the same thing somewhere else; it means filling in the deployment and maintenance work: keep the execution records you need, and make every tool's permission explicit and controllable.

On the left are the sensors: trace lets you see each step, eval in CI tests every change automatically, and the cost dashboard shows where the money goes. This is the Trace, Eval, and Loop from the checklist "From demo to maintainable", in its cloud version.

On the right are permissions: least privilege, sandboxes, reviewing third-party Skills, keys in Secret Manager, and a person confirming before irreversible actions. The 2-C experiment is more dangerous in the cloud, because a deployed system may get real credentials and mailbox permissions.

This run's pre-launch check had no ❌, but still three ⚠️ items: model credentials, SQLite durability, and remote MCP. No error mark does not mean it can go straight live. The local HTTP demo succeeding and the deployment HOMEWORK_MCP_URL not being set are different checks.
